transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I suppose what brings me in is that I just feel like I’m always going, always up and moving, even when there’s no real reason to be. It’s not like I’m running marathons or anything, but even on a quiet day at home I’ll start with the garden club list, then I’m over at my knitting bag, then I suddenly remember the travel papers I meant to look through, and before I know it I haven’t really finished any one of them. It’s like I bounce from one thing to the next, and I can’t quite just settle into one thing calmly.
Do you find that you need less sleep than usual, or that you feel unusually energetic or upbeat, even when there’s no clear reason for it?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way, no. I mean, I’ve always had spells where I’m busy or my mind is sort of moving along, but I don’t think I’m sleeping less and feeling wonderful because of it, if that’s what you mean. I don’t get that “up on top of the world” feeling, at least not that I’ve noticed.

Sometimes I may look energetic because I’m puttering around from one thing to another, but it doesn’t feel like some big burst of cheerfulness or like I don’t need rest. It’s more just… I’m restless, or I have trouble settling, but not especially upbeat for no reason.
Do you find that you get easily distracted or have trouble staying focused on a single task because your mind shifts quickly to something else?

Yes, I do, and it can be over the smallest things. I’ll be trying to read a letter or make a little list, and if someone is talking in the next room—even not loudly, just enough that I can hear the murmur—my mind sort of goes right over there. I’ll start wondering what they’re saying, or I’ll just lose the thread of what I was doing completely.

Or if a car goes by the window, especially if I catch the movement out of the corner of my eye, I’ll look up, and then somehow I’m not where I was anymore. I have to go back and reread the same line or stand there thinking, “Now what was I doing?” It’s not dramatic, exactly, but it happens often enough that it’s frustrating.
Do you find that these difficulties with focusing or getting distracted interfere with your ability to complete tasks, manage your time, or keep track of responsibilities in your daily life?

Yes, it does, and I wish I could say it was just a little nuisance, but it’s started to cause real strain. At home, my husband will think I’ve written something down or remembered what we agreed on, and then I’ll have it mixed up or not have followed through the way I meant to. Then he ends up checking behind me, which makes me feel embarrassed and a bit irritated too, even though I know he’s trying to help.

And at the community center, it’s similar. I’ll say I can help with a plan or keep track of something for the volunteers, and then someone has to remind me or double-check the details because they can’t really count on me to keep it all straight on my own. It’s not that I don’t care—I do care—but things slip or get tangled, and then other people have to pick up the loose ends. That’s been hard to admit.
Do you often feel worried, tense, or on edge, even when there isn’t a specific problem to solve?

I don’t think so, not in that constant way. I mean, I worry about ordinary things, like if I’ve forgotten something or if someone is expecting me to do something and I’m not sure I’ve got it right, but I wouldn’t say I’m sitting around tense all day for no reason.

Sometimes I can get a little keyed up if there’s something I’m supposed to handle, but if there isn’t a particular problem, I’m not usually just on edge out of nowhere. At least, I haven’t really noticed that as a main thing.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy, even for small periods of time?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I mean, I have days where I feel discouraged, especially when I’ve messed something up or I feel like I’ve disappointed someone, but I don’t think I’ve been feeling hopeless. Not in a heavy, constant sort of way.

And I still enjoy things, I think. Maybe I get frustrated with myself and then I don’t feel like doing much for a bit, but it doesn’t feel like I’ve lost interest in everything. It’s more that I get worn out by trying to keep up with things, and then I need to sit quietly or I just don’t feel very cheerful for a while. But I wouldn’t say I’ve been feeling down all the time, or that nothing gives me pleasure.
Looking back, would you say that these difficulties with focusing or feeling restless have been present since you were a child, even as far back as when you were in school?

Yes, I think so. Looking back, it wasn’t just something that started recently. Even when I was in grade school, my teachers would tell my mother that I was bright, but scattered — that was the word that seemed to come up. I remember hearing that sort of thing, or my mother repeating it, like, “You’re smart, but you don’t keep track of things.”

I was always losing papers, or I’d forget to bring something home, or I’d have the work partly done and then somehow it wouldn’t get turned in. And I talked out of turn a lot, not always meaning to be rude, but I’d just blurt things out. I also remember wiggling in my seat, like I’d be ready to be done before I had actually finished the work in front of me. So yes, when I think back on it, there were signs of this when I was a child.
